newsitem.title: UK: IRA calls truce, N.Ireland Unionists sceptical.
newsitem.headline: IRA calls truce, N.Ireland Unionists sceptical.

text.p: The IRA on Saturday announced a new truce in its 28-year war against British rule in Northern Ireland which will take effect at midday on Sunday and allow its Sinn Fein spokesmen a seat at peace talks.
The move was welcomed by British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who said his government would asses it "with great care" to ensure it met British demands for a commitment to peace.
The truce was announced in a statement to Irish state broadcaster RTE. It said "all IRA units have been instructed accordingly" and would be stood down.

"The IRA is committed to ending British rule in Ireland. It is the root cause of division and conflict in our country. We want a permanent peace and therefore we are prepared to enhance the search for a democratic peace settlement through real and inclusive political negotiations," the statement said.

The truce replaces a ceasefire the guerrillas called in 1994 in response to an Anglo-Irish peace inititative but which they broke with a bomb attack in London in February 1996 after failing to earn a seat at the peace negotiations.
Initial reaction from the IRA's mirror-opposites, Unionists representing a 60 percent Protestant majority which wants the province to remain British, ranged from derision to caution.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the hardline Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), hinted at a walkout of the talks. "No unionist of any standing...will be sitting down along with them," he told the BBC.

He was furious that under new British guidelines, Sinn Fein will be able to take part in talks on a lasting settlement without handing in any weapons or "decommsioning" its two-tonne stock of automatic weapons and plastic explosives.
Ken Maginniss, security spokesman for the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party, said he welcomed the truce if it was real.

"We cannot forget the difficulties that arose in 1994 when we got a ceasefire which was basically a three-month ceasefire extended month by month as the IRA demanded and threatened when they wanted concessions at every turn," he said.

Parties to the negotiations, which have excluded Sinn Fein until now, must vote next Wednesday on Anglo-Irish proposals that the guerrillas surrender weapons as the talks progress, rather than before or at the end of the negotiations.
The UUP's Jeffrey Donaldson said his party leader, David Trimble, plan to hold talks with Blair on Monday to clear up the decommissioning issue.

"We will want to know whether the government is prepared to chance the document on decommissioning which is to be voted on next Wednesday. We are deeply concerned that the government has done a secret deal with the IRA to secure another ceasefire," Donaldson said.
The IRA statement said: "We have ordered the unequivocal restoration of the ceasefire of August 1994."
It was the first time the IRA had used the word "unequivocal" and met British demands for an unconditional end to its war.
Britain says the issue of "decommissioning", which has snarled the peace talks since they began 13 months ago, can be handled in parallel negotiations.
Blair's government has also promised to review the issue of hundreds of IRA prisoners in British jails for security offences linked to a three-decade-old conflict that has killed 3,200.
It also says it will put a time-frame on the talks between Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists of the end of May next year so that they do not drag on endlessly.

For the past two years the IRA has baulked at any demand that it hand over the semtex plastic explosive and arsenal of automatic weapons it has used to attack what it sees as Britain's occupation of a part of Ireland.
